questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Causes of simple goitre in hilly regions
questions.question: Simple goitre is usually seen in people living in the hilly regions. Give two reasons for the statement.
questions.solution: Correct answer: (a) The soil and water of hilly regions are deficient in iodine, so people there get insufficient iodine in their diet. (b) Without iodine the thyroid cannot make enough thyroxine; low thyroxine removes the negative feedback on the pituitary, which secretes excess TSH, making the thyroid gland enlarge (simple goitre). Printed key: (a) 'Increased ATP demand triggers the negative feedback regulation of thyroid hormone secretion' (not accurate); (b) insufficient iodine in the soil of hilly areas also causes goitre. Accept either wording of the iodine-deficiency reason.

marking_points.point: Soil/water/food of hilly regions is deficient in iodine (insufficient dietary iodine)
Lack of iodine -> less thyroxine -> excess TSH/negative feedback loss -> thyroid gland enlarges (goitre)

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
concepts: adrenal virilism from excess adrenal androgens
questions.question: What is Adrenal Virilism? What causes this condition?
questions.solution: Adrenal virilism is a condition in which a female develops male secondary sexual characteristics (beard, moustache, deepening and hoarsening of voice). It is caused by excess production of androgens from the adrenal cortex in females.

marking_points.point: Definition: females develop male secondary sexual characters (beard, moustache, deep voice)
Cause: excess secretion of androgens by adrenal cortex

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
concepts: retina and image formation at the yellow spot (fovea)
questions.question: Which is the light sensitive layer of the eyeball? Where exactly is the image formed on this layer?
questions.solution: The retina is the light-sensitive layer (has photoreceptors rods and cones). The image is formed on the yellow spot (macula lutea/fovea centralis) of the retina. Printed key says 'Image is formed in front of retina', which is factually incorrect for a normal eye; accept yellow spot / fovea / macula.

marking_points.point: Retina
Image formed on the yellow spot (fovea centralis/macula lutea) of the retina

questions.question: Study the diagram given below and answer the questions that follow: (a) Identify the defect of the eye by mentioning the technical term. (b) Mention one reason for this defect. (c) Name the type of lens used to correct this defect.
questions.solution: (a) Hypermetropia (hyperopia, long-sightedness). (b) Eyeball is too short, or the lens cannot become round (convex) enough, so the image forms behind the retina. (c) Convex lens.

marking_points.point: Hypermetropia / hyperopia / long-sightedness
Reason: eyeball too short or eye lens too flat/weak (cannot converge enough)
Convex lens

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
questions.topic: Synapse; cytons and axons in cerebrum
concepts: grey and white matter in cerebrum
questions.question: Define the term Synapse. How are Cytons and Axons of neurons placed in the Cerebrum?
questions.solution: Synapse is the site of transmission of nerve impulses between two neurons, or between a neuron and an effector (gland/muscle cell). In the cerebrum the cytons (cell bodies) lie in the outer layer (cortex, grey matter), while the axons (nerve fibres) lie in the inner portion (white matter).

marking_points.point: Synapse: junction/site of transmission of nerve impulse between two neurons (or neuron and effector)
Cytons are in the outer layer (cortex) - grey matter
Axons are in the inner portion - white matter

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B

questions.solution: Meninges: dura mater (outer), arachnoid mater (middle), pia mater (inner). Printed key lists arachnoid as inner and pia as middle, which is the wrong order; accept the three names in any order.

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
concepts: RBC adaptation: no nucleus or mitochondria, more haemoglobin
questions.question: A mature mammalian erythrocyte lacks nucleus and mitochondria but is efficient in its functioning. Explain by giving suitable reasons.
questions.solution: Lack of nucleus and mitochondria makes room for more haemoglobin and hence carries more oxygen. It also gives the cell its biconcave shape, which increases surface area for efficient diffusion of gases. (Mitochondria absent so the RBC does not consume the oxygen it carries; young RBCs have a nucleus.)

marking_points.point: More space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen carried
Biconcave shape / larger surface area for efficient diffusion of gases

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
questions.question: The diagram given below is that of a human brain, with parts numbered 1, 2 and 3. Answer the questions that follow: (a) Label the parts numbered 2 and 3. (b) State any one function of the part numbered 1.
questions.solution: (a) 2 - Cerebellum; 3 - Medulla oblongata. (b) Part 1 is the cerebrum; it initiates and coordinates voluntary movement, and is the seat of intelligence, memory, thinking, will power; (printed key: initiates and coordinates movement and regulates body temperature).

marking_points.point: 2 - Cerebellum
3 - Medulla oblongata
Any one function of cerebrum (voluntary movement, intelligence, memory, thinking, etc.)

questions.figure_desc: Side view of the human brain with three parts numbered: 1 = cerebrum, 2 = cerebellum, 3 = medulla oblongata.

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
questions.question: What is a reflex action? Name the two types of reflexes.
questions.solution: Reflex action is a rapid, automatic response to a stimulus, not under voluntary control of the brain. Two types: natural (unconditioned/simple) reflexes and conditioned (acquired) reflexes.

marking_points.point: Reflex action: rapid, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus
Natural/unconditioned (simple) reflex
Conditioned/acquired reflex

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
questions.question: Give the exact location of Pulmonary semilunar valve. When does it close?
questions.solution: It is located at the opening of the right ventricle into the pulmonary artery. It closes during ventricular diastole (when the ventricle relaxes), preventing backflow of blood into the ventricle.

marking_points.point: Location: at the opening of right ventricle into pulmonary artery
Closes at ventricular diastole (relaxation)

questions.choice_note: any 3 of 5 questions in Section B
concepts: functions of lymphocytes, platelets and neutrophils
questions.question: Mention one function for each of the following: (a) Lymphocytes (b) Thrombocytes (c) Neutrophils
questions.solution: (a) Lymphocytes: immune response, antibody production, killing virus-infected and tumour cells. (b) Thrombocytes: help blood clotting to stop bleeding and heal wounds. (c) Neutrophils: phagocytosis - ingest and destroy bacteria and fungi.

marking_points.point: Lymphocytes: antibody production / immune response
Thrombocytes: blood clotting
Neutrophils: phagocytosis of pathogens
